title: Inter-State Disputes

cards.h: When two states claim the same river
cards.b:
Inter-state disputes test whether federalism is a partnership or a tug of war. Water is the oldest and hardest issue. The rivers cross state lines, but water is a State List subject (Entry 17), while inter-state rivers fall under the Union List (Entry 56).

Disputes also arise over borders, capitals, sharing of power projects and migration. Examiners ask three kinds of question: the legal machinery, the main cases (Cauvery, Krishna, Ravi-Beas) and whether the system works.

Remember the core tension. A state sees its river water as a matter of life and votes. The Union has to act as neutral referee. When parties see the Union as partisan, trust falls.

Mind map of this lesson

Water: Art. 262 and the 1956 Act. Courts: Art. 131. Talk: Art. 263 and Zonal Councils. Borders: Belagavi and Northeast. Fix: commissions and the 2019 Bill.

cards.h: Four constitutional doors for dispute resolution
cards.b:
1. Article 262: Parliament may by law provide for settling disputes over inter-state rivers and may bar courts from hearing them. Parliament used this in the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 and the River Boards Act, 1956 (never used).
  2. Article 131: the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in disputes between the Union and states, or between states. A proviso keeps out disputes arising from certain pre-Constitution treaties and agreements.
  3. Article 263: the President can set up an Inter-State Council to inquire into disputes and advise. It was created in 1990 after the Sarkaria Commission.
  4. Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act, 1956): five zones, chaired by the Union Home Minister. Their talk can settle border and power-sharing issues. The North Eastern Council (1971) serves the Northeast.

Other tools: Article 307 (an inter-state trade commission, never created) and Articles 301 to 304 on free trade within the country.

cards.h: How the water tribunal route works
cards.b:
The 1956 Act says: the Centre first tries negotiation. If that fails, it can set up a tribunal. The 2002 amendment set a three-year target (extendable by two years) and made the award as binding as a Supreme Court order.

Article 262 bars courts from hearing the dispute, yet the Supreme Court has still heard challenges as special leave petitions (Article 136), and in Cauvery (2018) it modified the award.

The conflict goes back to treaties of 1892 and 1924 between Madras Presidency and Mysore. After independence, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu disagreed.

  • 1990: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal formed. An interim order in 1991 led to riots in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
  • 1991-93: Karnataka's ordinance against the order was held void in In re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1993), a reference under Article 143.
  • 2007: Tribunal's final award; Kerala and Puducherry also got shares.
  • 16 February 2018: the Supreme Court reduced Tamil Nadu's share, raised Karnataka's by 14.75 TMC to 284.75 TMC, and declared the river a national asset. It also ordered a Cauvery Water Management Authority (set up June 2018).

Distress years, when the monsoon fails, remain the flashpoint. Karnataka's Mekedatu reservoir plan is another trigger.

• Krishna: KWDT-I (Bachawat, 1976) and KWDT-II (Brijesh Kumar, 2010, further report 2013) among Maharashtra, Karnataka and undivided Andhra. After Telangana's creation (2014), Andhra and Telangana quarrel over sharing; the Centre referred it to the existing Tribunal.
  • Ravi-Beas: 1981 agreement among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan; Eradi Tribunal 1986. Punjab passed the Termination of Agreements Act, 2004. A Presidential reference (Article 143) led the Supreme Court in 2016 to find it invalid. The SYL canal remains unfinished. In 2025 Punjab and Haryana again clashed over Bhakra water releases.
  • Narmada: tribunal award of 1979 across Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed Sardar Sarovar on displacement grounds.
  • Mahadayi: Goa, Karnataka and Maharashtra; tribunal award 2018.
  • Mullaperiyar: Kerala and Tamil Nadu over a 1886 lease; Supreme Court allowed 142 ft storage in 2014.

• Belagavi: Maharashtra claims this Karnataka district. The Mahajan Commission (1966) favoured Karnataka's hold. Maharashtra rejected it.
  • Chandigarh and Punjab-Haryana: shared capital since 1966. The Rajiv-Longowal Accord (1985) promised transfer to Punjab, still unmet.
  • Assam's borders with Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal. The worst clash was Assam-Mizoram on 26 July 2021, when six Assam police personnel died. Assam and Meghalaya signed a deal on 29 March 2022 to settle six of twelve disputed areas, and Assam and Arunachal reached an agreement in 2023.
  • Ladakh, Telangana, Andhra: division of assets after bifurcation (Schedules 9 and 10 of the 2014 Act).

The Centre has no clear tool to redraw borders by agreement; Article 3 gives power to Parliament, but political consent is needed.

Sarkaria Commission (1988)

Wanted a standing Inter-State Council under Article 263 and early consultation, so conflicts need not reach the courts.

Punchhi Commission (2010)

Urged that Zonal Councils and the Inter-State Council be used more actively and that disputes be settled faster.

Ramaswamy R. Iyer, Water: Perspectives, Issues, Concerns (2003)

Argued that water should be treated as a shared resource and that basin-wide negotiation is better than quarrel over shares.

Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2019

Proposed a permanent tribunal with several benches and a dispute resolution committee to try negotiation first. The Lok Sabha passed it in 2019, but the Rajya Sabha did not, so it lapsed with the 17th Lok Sabha. I could not confirm a fresh bill since then.

• Delays: Cauvery took 17 years in the tribunal and 11 more to a final Supreme Court ruling.
  • Compliance: states defy orders when public anger is high, as Karnataka did in 1991 and Punjab in 2004.
  • Politics: the Centre acts as a party when the same party or alliance rules different states. Opposition states call it biased.
  • Legal gaps: Article 262 is awkward since the Court still gets involved. A single permanent tribunal might solve this but also centralises power.
  • Climate and data: unreliable water data and climate stress make "equitable apportionment" harder.

A cooperative answer: a technical basin authority, real-time data and compensation for the losing state, instead of one-time awards.

• Cauvery in lean years: disputes returned in September 2023 when Karnataka was short of rain and the CWMA ordered releases.
  • Krishna: the Centre referred a Telangana-Andhra reallocation request to KWDT-II in October 2023.
  • Punjab-Haryana water (2025) and the Bhakra Beas Management Board.
  • Indus Waters Treaty: India put it "in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025. This is an international dispute, but it shows the same principle: a river is shared.
  • Northeast borders: Assam-Meghalaya, Assam-Arunachal agreements show talk can work.
  • Federal ties: the Supreme Court's 2025 rulings on Governors and the GST Council show the broader theme of Centre-state trust.

quiz.q: Which Article lets Parliament provide for settling inter-state river disputes?
The Inter-State Council is created by…
Water as a subject falls in…
o: State List Entry 17, with inter-state rivers regulated under Union List Entry 56
quiz.w: Water is in the State List, subject to Union control of inter-state rivers.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court's 2018 Cauvery verdict gave Karnataka…
quiz.w: It raised Karnataka's share by 14.75 TMC to 284.75 TMC.

quiz.q: The Cauvery Water Management Authority was set up in…
quiz.w: Created in June 2018 after the Supreme Court ordered a scheme.

quiz.q: The Punjab Termination of Agreements Act, 2004 related to…
quiz.w: It was held invalid on a Presidential reference in 2016.
